title: The Professor Who Counted Pins
book: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith
wiifm: Every pound your businesses earn passes through a machine nobody designed: strangers specialising, trading and chasing prices up and down. Adam Smith was the first person to describe that machine whole, and he did it as an absent-minded Scottish bachelor who lived most of his life with his mother. You will follow him from a fishing town in Fife to the salons of Paris and back to a desk in Kirkcaldy, and you will come away knowing what really creates wealth, what limits how far you can specialise, and why the father of free markets trusted businessmen less than almost anyone.

ch.h: The boy the travellers gave back
b: Adam Smith never met his father. The elder Adam Smith, a customs official in the small port of Kirkcaldy on the Firth of Forth, died a few months before his son was born, and the boy was baptised on the fifth of June 1723. He was raised by his mother, Margaret Douglas, a capable woman from a landed Fife family, and the two of them were so close that he lived with her for most of the next sixty years. He never married. She died in 1784, and he said afterwards that she had certainly loved him more than any other person ever had or ever would.

There is one famous story from those years. When he was about three, visiting his uncle at Strathendry, he was carried off by a passing band of travellers, the people the eighteenth century called gypsies. His uncle gave chase and the child was found abandoned in a wood. The story comes from his first biographer, Dugald Stewart, and the Victorian biographer John Rae added the dry verdict that the boy would have made, one fears, a poor gypsy.

He was sickly, bookish and given to talking to himself. At the burgh school he did well enough that at fourteen, in 1737, he was sent to the University of Glasgow. There he fell under the spell of Francis Hutcheson, a moral philosopher who lectured in English rather than Latin and taught that human beings are naturally sociable creatures. Smith called him the never to be forgotten Hutcheson. The question Hutcheson planted, how a society of self-interested people holds together at all, would occupy Smith for the rest of his life.
ch.cap: Adam's uncle finds the boy left in the wood

b: In 1740 Smith won the Snell Exhibition scholarship and rode south to Balliol College, Oxford. He stayed six years and was mostly miserable. The Scots were unpopular, the food was bad, and the teaching, he later wrote, had more or less stopped. In the greater part of the university, he said, the public professors had for many years given up altogether even the pretence of teaching.

This is worth noticing, because it is the first appearance of an idea that runs through the whole of The Wealth of Nations. Oxford professors were paid from endowments, whatever they did. Their income did not depend on whether a single student learned anything. So they did nothing. Smith never forgot it. When he came to write about institutions, he always asked the same question first: who is paid, and for what? It is the question a good manager still asks of every incentive scheme.

What he did do was read enormously on his own, in Greek, Latin, French and English, with nobody examining him. He came home in 1746 without any clear plan, and for two years he lived with his mother in Kirkcaldy and read.
ch.cap: Smith reads alone while his Oxford professor sleeps

ch.h: The professor and the impartial spectator
b: His break came through public lectures in Edinburgh from 1748, on rhetoric and then on law. They were a success, and in 1751 Glasgow made him Professor of Logic, and the following year Professor of Moral Philosophy, Hutcheson's old chair. Glasgow's merchants were growing rich on American tobacco, and Smith dined and argued with them.

His first book, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, appeared in 1759 and made his name across Europe. It is not about money at all. It asks how we come to have a conscience, and its answer is that we learn to judge ourselves by imagining how we look to an impartial spectator, a fair and well informed observer inside our own heads. This matters for understanding the later book. The man who wrote about self-interest had first written a whole volume on sympathy. He never thought people were only selfish. He thought commerce let even selfish people cooperate.

In a lecture of 1755, reported after his death by Stewart, he said that little else was needed to carry a state from the lowest barbarism to the highest opulence but peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice. People quote that line as the thesis of The Wealth of Nations. It is genuine Smith, but it is not in that book at all.
ch.cap: Smith lectures on the impartial spectator inside us

ch.h: A book to pass the time
b: In 1764 Smith gave up his professorship for a far better paid job: travelling tutor to the young Duke of Buccleuch. The salary of three hundred pounds a year, for life, would make him independent. The two men set off for France.

They began in Toulouse, where Smith knew almost nobody and spoke poor French, and he was bored. In a letter to Hume that summer he wrote that he had begun to write a book in order to pass away the time. That book became The Wealth of Nations.

They travelled to Geneva, where Smith met Voltaire, and in 1766 to Paris, where the conversations changed him. He met François Quesnay, physician to the king, and the circle of economists called the Physiocrats, who believed that a whole economy could be studied as a system with its own circulation, like blood in a body. He met Anne Robert Jacques Turgot, later finance minister, who was working on the same problems. Stewart reports that Smith intended to dedicate his book to Quesnay, who died before it appeared.

It is important to be honest here. Smith did not invent every idea he is famous for. Much of the raw material, from the division of labour to free trade, was in the air in Paris and Edinburgh. What he supplied was the synthesis: one long, readable, evidence-heavy account of an economy as a single self-organising machine.
The journey ended in grief. In October 1766 the duke's younger brother, Hew Campbell Scott, fell ill and died in Paris, and Smith brought the party home.
ch.cap: Bored in Toulouse, Smith starts a book to pass time

ch.h: Ten men and forty-eight thousand pins
b: Back in Kirkcaldy, Smith settled into his mother's house and wrote, slowly, for about ten years. The book opens with a pin.

He describes a small workshop where ten men make pins. One draws out the wire, another straightens it, a third cuts it, a fourth points it, a fifth grinds the top to receive the head. Making the head takes two or three more operations. Whitening the pins is a trade of its own, and so is putting them into paper. About eighteen distinct operations in all. Between them, he says, the ten men could make about twelve pounds of pins a day, upwards of forty-eight thousand pins. Working alone, each doing all eighteen steps, they could not each have made twenty, perhaps not one.

Smith says he had seen such a workshop. Historians have pointed out that his eighteen operations match, almost exactly, the article on pins in the great French Encyclopédie of the 1750s, which he owned. So the scene is partly observation and partly reading. The arithmetic is the point either way: same people, same day, thousands of times the output, purely from how the work is arranged.

He then explains why, and his three reasons still hold. First, dexterity: do one thing ten thousand times and you get fast at it. Second, the time lost switching between tasks, including what he called sauntering, the slack and careless attention of a mind that has just changed jobs. That is context switching, described two and a half centuries early. Third, and he thought this the most important, a worker fixed on one narrow task starts inventing better ways to do it. Specialise first, and the machines follow from the hands of the people doing the work.
ch.cap: Ten men split eighteen steps and make 48,000 pins

ch.h: The butcher, the brewer and the baker
b: If everyone specialises, everyone depends on strangers for nearly everything. Why does that not end in chaos? Smith's answer in his second chapter is the most quoted passage in economics. It is not, he writes, from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.

People usually stop there and hear a celebration of greed. Read on and it is something subtler: a lesson in persuasion. We address ourselves, he says, not to their humanity but to their self-love, and never talk to them of our own necessities but of their advantages. When you want cooperation from a stranger, do not tell them what you need. Tell them what they get. A commercial society is one where you can obtain the help of thousands of people who do not know you and owe you nothing. Smith thought that a remarkable moral achievement.

Then comes the idea most readers miss, in a chapter titled, in effect, that the division of labour is limited by the extent of the market. A porter can make a living in a big town but not in a village, because there is not enough carrying to do. In the remote Highlands every farmer must be his own butcher, baker and brewer, not because Highlanders are backward but because the market is too thin to support specialists.

This is why Smith was so interested in water. A broad-wheeled waggon with two men and eight horses took about six weeks to carry four tons from London to Edinburgh and back. A ship with six or eight men carried two hundred tons in the same time. Cheap transport widens the market, a wider market supports more specialists, and more specialists produce more wealth. For any business owner, it explains why you cannot yet afford the specialist you know you need: your market is not yet large enough to pay for them.
ch.cap: The butcher, brewer and baker each serve their own interest

ch.h: The price that keeps coming back
b: Smith's next step turned a pile of observations into a system. He separated two kinds of price. The market price is what a thing actually fetches today, set by how much is brought to market against how many people want it. The natural price is the price that just covers the rent, wages and profit needed to bring it to market at the ordinary rates of the area. Sell at the natural price and you are neither making a killing nor slowly going bust.

The market price, he wrote, is continually gravitating towards the natural price. When it rises above it, the extra profit acts like an advertisement. Capital and workers move in, supply grows, and the price is pulled back down. When it falls below, people lose money, they leave, supply shrinks and the price recovers. Nobody decides how many bakers a town needs. The signal does it.

Two consequences follow. First, unusually high profit is self-destroying in the normal case, so anything that earns above the ordinary rate for years is being protected by something: a secret, a patent, a monopoly, a royal charter. Second, the mechanism only works if people and money can move. Smith attacked everything in Britain that stopped them: apprenticeship laws demanding seven years before a man could practise a trade, guilds that limited membership, and settlement rules that made it hard for a poor labourer to move parish to find work.

Now the phrase everyone associates with him. Smith used the words invisible hand only once in The Wealth of Nations, in Book Four, about why merchants prefer to invest at home rather than abroad. He used it once in The Theory of Moral Sentiments and once in an early essay on astronomy. Three uses in a lifetime of writing. Scholars such as Emma Rothschild have even argued he meant it a little ironically. The mechanism he described is real. The slogan is mostly a later invention.
ch.cap: The market price swings back toward the natural price

ch.h: The real villain was the merchant
b: From 1773 Smith lived in London, polishing the manuscript and watching the quarrel with the American colonies boil over. The Wealth of Nations was published on the ninth of March 1776, four months before the American Declaration of Independence. It was not a defence of business. It was an attack on a system, which Smith called the mercantile system.

Mercantilism held that a country grew rich by piling up gold and silver, so exports were good, imports were bad, and government should rig trade to favour home producers. Britain ran on it: tariffs, export bounties, the Navigation Acts, and colonies forced to buy only from the mother country. Smith's reply was one sentence. Consumption, he wrote, is the sole end and purpose of all production. Wealth is not gold in a vault. It is the goods and services people can actually use. Once you accept that, a tariff that protects a producer is simply a tax on every customer.

He was scathing about who wrote these rules. People of the same trade, he wrote, seldom meet together, even for merriment, but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance to raise prices. He did not want such meetings banned, which he thought impossible in a free country. He wanted the law to stop making them easy. He warned that any new law proposed by merchants should be examined with the greatest suspicion, because it came from people whose interest was never exactly the same as the public's.

He even foresaw the problem of the modern company. Directors of joint-stock companies, managing other people's money rather than their own, could not be expected to watch it with the same anxious care, so negligence and waste would always prevail. His great example was the East India Company, a private business with its own army that had plundered Bengal. Building an empire to create customers, he wrote, might seem a project fit only for a nation of shopkeepers. The phrase was his, long before Napoleon borrowed it.
ch.cap: Merchants of one trade huddle, conspiring against the public

ch.h: The free trader who collected customs
b: In 1778 Smith accepted a post as a Commissioner of Customs in Edinburgh. It looks like a joke: the great critic of tariffs spending his last years enforcing them. He took it seriously, attending the board several days a week. Around 1780 he wrote to a friend that, having checked the list of prohibited imports, he found that almost every scarf, ruffle and handkerchief he owned was contraband, and he burned the lot to set a good example.

He also kept revising. The final book of The Wealth of Nations sets out what government should actually do, and it is far from the caricature of a man who wanted no state. The sovereign has three duties: defence, justice, and public works and institutions that benefit society but which no individual could profit from building. Under that last heading he placed roads, bridges, harbours and, surprisingly to many, schooling for ordinary children, paid for largely in public.

His reason is the darkest passage in the book, and it is aimed at his own central idea. A man whose whole life is spent performing a few simple operations, he wrote, generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become. The division of labour that makes nations rich makes individual workers narrow. Smith saw both halves and refused to hide the second. Education was his remedy for the damage his own engine caused.

He added four rules for good taxes that are still taught: taxes should match people's ability to pay, be certain rather than arbitrary, be due at a convenient time, and cost little to collect. As tests go, nobody has bettered them.

In the summer of 1790, knowing he was dying, he asked his friends Joseph Black and James Hutton to burn his unpublished manuscripts. They reported destroying some sixteen volumes. He died at Panmure House in Edinburgh on the seventeenth of July 1790, aged sixty-seven, having published two books in his lifetime and judged everything else unworthy to survive him.
ch.cap: Customs Commissioner Smith burns his own contraband scarves

ch.h: What he got wrong, and what lasted
b: Smith deserves an honest reckoning. His theory of value wobbles between labour, cost of production and market price, and never settles; it took the marginalist economists of the 1870s to sort it out. His story of money, that people first bartered and then invented coins to solve the inconvenience, has been attacked hard by anthropologists, most prominently David Graeber, who argued that no society has been found running on barter the way Smith describes, and that credit and obligation came first. He also underrated the joint-stock company, thinking it suited only to routine trades like banking and insurance. It went on to build the industrial world.

But the core has lasted. Wealth is the flow of useful things people can consume, not a hoard of money. It grows when people specialise and trade. How far they can specialise is set by the size of the market. Prices act as signals that move capital and labour to where they are wanted, and above-normal profit is either temporary or protected by something. And the people most eager to protect it, by persuading government to build walls around their trade, are businessmen themselves.

That last point sets up the rest of the week. Smith described a machine that competes profit away and treated the exceptions as distortions to be swept aside. Tomorrow's author, Peter Thiel, read the same machine and concluded that the exceptions are the only part worth having.
ch.cap: Smith's bronze statue stands on Edinburgh's Royal Mile

take: Take one process a single person owns end to end and list every operation, as Smith did with the pin. You will usually find one or two steps eat most of the time and that switching between tasks is quietly costing you more than effort.
Your market sets your hiring plan

The division of labour is limited by the extent of the market. For each role you wish you could fill, write the monthly volume at which it pays for itself, and favour growth moves that shorten the distance to it.

Smith's baker lesson is about persuasion: never talk of your own needs, talk of the other person's gain. Rewrite your next pitch, advert or partnership email so every sentence is about what the reader gets.
Profit above the ordinary rate attracts competitors unless something genuinely blocks them. If you earn an unusual margin, name the barrier protecting it; if you cannot, plan for it to shrink.
Ask who is paid, and for what
Oxford professors paid regardless of teaching stopped teaching. Check every incentive in your business by what it literally pays for, not what you hoped it would produce.
Smith warned that proposals from businessmen deserve the greatest suspicion. When an argument conveniently protects your own position, test it twice as hard as one that costs you.

The same division of labour that makes firms productive can make jobs narrow and dulling. Rotate, train and explain the bigger picture so specialists do not become, in Smith's harsh phrase, stupid and ignorant.
Take the shape, check the details
Smith got money's origins and the theory of value wrong but the overall mechanism right. Use great thinkers for their structure and verify their specific claims yourself.
recall: What were Smith's three reasons that the division of labour raises output?

Greater dexterity from repetition, time saved by not switching between tasks, which he called avoiding sauntering, and the invention of better methods and machines by workers focused on one narrow job. He thought the third the most important.
What limits how far work can be divided, and why did Smith care about water?

The extent of the market: a specialist can only exist where there is enough demand to keep them busy, which is why a village cannot support a porter. Water transport hugely enlarged markets, since a ship moved two hundred tons in the time a waggon moved four, so wealth grew along coasts and rivers.
How many times does the invisible hand appear in The Wealth of Nations, and what is that passage about?
Once, in Book Four, about why merchants prefer to invest their capital at home rather than abroad. He used the phrase only twice more in all his published work.
What did Smith say about people of the same trade meeting together, and what did he prescribe?

That their conversation tends to end in a conspiracy against the public or a scheme to raise prices. He thought such meetings could not be banned in a free country, but argued the law should not make them easier.
Why did Smith want the state to pay for ordinary children's education?

Because he believed the division of labour, which made nations rich, could leave a worker who did a few simple operations all his life as stupid and ignorant as a person could become. Schooling was his remedy for that damage, alongside defence, justice and public works as the state's duties.

stories: The boy who would have made a poor gypsy

Adam Smith, the man who explained how strangers cooperate, was nearly raised by strangers himself. At about three, visiting his uncle at Strathendry in Fife, he was carried off by a passing band of travellers, the people the eighteenth century called gypsies. His uncle gave chase, and the boy was found abandoned in a wood. The story comes from his first biographer, Dugald Stewart, and the Victorian biographer John Rae added the perfect line: the child would have made, one fears, a poor gypsy. He was sickly, bookish and given to talking to himself. Economics nearly lost its founder before he could read.

The most important book in economics opens not with gold or kings but with a pin. Smith describes a small workshop of ten men. One draws the wire, one straightens it, one cuts it, one points it, one grinds the top for the head, and so on through about eighteen steps. Together they make upwards of forty-eight thousand pins a day. Working alone, each doing every step, they might not make twenty, perhaps not one. Same people, same day, thousands of times the output, purely from how the work is arranged. The twist: his eighteen steps match the French Encyclopédie's article on pins almost exactly, so the famous scene was probably partly borrowed from his bookshelf.
The free trader who burned his scarves

Smith spent his life arguing against tariffs and import bans. So what job did he take in 1778? Commissioner of Customs in Edinburgh, enforcing them. He did it conscientiously, attending the board several days a week. The story goes that around 1780 he read the official list of prohibited imports and realised that almost every scarf, ruffle and handkerchief he owned was contraband. So, he wrote to a friend, he burned the lot to set a good example. Historians treat the tale with some caution. But it captures the man perfectly: he disagreed with the rules, and he still kept them.
biz: Write out the pin steps for one lead

Smith counted eighteen steps in a pin. Do the same for one secured loan enquiry: ad click, form, first call, WhatsApp follow up, fact find, document chase, lender submission, offer. This week, time each step on ten real cases and note every handover and every time someone switches task. Smith's sauntering is the minutes lost each time an adviser jumps from a call to a document chase and back. Measure time from enquiry to first contact and from fact find to submission. Fix the slowest step first, and keep the customer's need for clear, unhurried explanations untouched.

Smith's baker lesson is that you win strangers by talking about their interest, not your needs. Rewrite one ad, one landing page and your first WhatsApp message so every line answers what the homeowner actually gets: lenders compared for them, the risks of securing debt on their home explained plainly, no fee surprises. Consumer Duty makes this a test, not a slogan, so keep representative examples prominent and never imply approval or rates are assured. For Debt Support Direct, lead with what free, regulated help looks like. Measure enquiry quality, not just volume.
connects: Thiel takes Smith's insight that competition drives profit down to the ordinary rate and concludes that the only businesses worth building are the protected exceptions.
Smith's market price constantly gravitating back to the natural price is an early description of a self-correcting feedback loop of the kind systems thinking studies.
Smith's advice to address a stranger's self-love rather than your own needs is the seed of the persuasion principles Cialdini later tested.
recap:
Adam Smith never met his father. He was born in the little Scottish port of Kirkcaldy in seventeen twenty-three, a few months after his father died, and he lived with his mother for most of his life. At three, the story goes, he was carried off by travellers and found abandoned in a wood. At fourteen he went to Glasgow, where a teacher called Francis Hutcheson planted the question of his life: how does a society of self-interested people hold together at all?

Oxford gave him a first clue by accident. His professors were paid whatever they did, so they did nothing. Smith never forgot it. Ask who is paid, and for what.

He became a celebrated professor, wrote a book about conscience and sympathy, then took a well paid post tutoring a young duke in France. Bored in Toulouse, he began a book to pass the time. Twelve years later, in seventeen seventy-six, it appeared as The Wealth of Nations.

It opens with a pin. Ten men, each doing a small part of eighteen steps, make forty-eight thousand pins a day. Alone, each might not make twenty. That is the first big idea: wealth comes from specialisation, from how work is arranged.

The second is that specialisation is limited by the size of the market. A village cannot keep a porter busy. That is why Smith loved ships and rivers. Cheap transport makes markets bigger, and bigger markets support more specialists.

The third is that prices are signals. When a price runs above its natural level, the extra profit acts like an advertisement, rivals pour in, and the price is pulled back down. Nobody plans how many bakers a town needs. So if a business earns unusual profits for years, something is protecting it.

The fourth surprises people. The father of free markets distrusted businessmen. He warned that people of the same trade seldom meet without the talk turning to a conspiracy against the public, and that any law merchants propose deserves the greatest suspicion.

The fifth is his honesty about the cost. A lifetime of simple, repetitive work can leave a person narrow and dulled, so he wanted ordinary children schooled at public expense.

Before he died in seventeen ninety his friends burned some sixteen volumes of his unfinished papers at his request. He got some things wrong. But the machine he described is the one we still live inside.

So remember this. We do not expect our dinner from the butcher's kindness, but from his interest, so talk to people about what they gain.
